title: Edge AI as a Factory Floor: Finding Bottlenecks and Keeping Data Moving
summary: Real-time inference faces a familiar operations problem: keep work moving through constrained stages. The solution may be a faster conveyor, another parallel path, or fewer unnecessary handoffs—not simply a faster processor. By Braden Cooper, Director of Products Section 1: Why Treat Real-Time Edge AI Like a Factory Floor? A real-time Edge AI pipeline behaves like a factory floor: data enters as demand, moves through constrained processing stages, waits when capacity falls short, and exits as detections, tracking vectors, or actuation commands. When one stage cannot keep pace, queues grow—and throughput, response time, and deterministic control suffer. The technology is different, but the flow problem is familiar: demand can exceed capacity, work can accumulate between stages, and one constrained resource can limit the entire system. That is why operations management provides a useful framework for Edge AI optimization. Bottleneck analysis, Little’s Law, demand distributions, and queuing theory apply here just as they do on a production line. They let us put numbers behind the traffic jam and decide what to change. Model and compute benchmarks matter, but they do not describe performance under real mission demand. A fast model cannot sustain its rated inference throughput when host-memory copies, interconnect contention, limited buffer capacity, or competing workloads delay the data it needs. The practical shift is from tuning components in isolation to optimizing the complete flow. That begins by mapping the pipeline and finding the constraint that governs end-to-end performance. At OSS, we use this framework to evaluate rugged Edge AI platforms as complete data pipelines. PCIe interconnects, switch fabrics, GPU and NVMe connectivity, scheduling, and thermal architecture must work together to sustain flow—not just deliver isolated benchmark results. Figure 1. Sensor demand moves through shared data paths, buffers, and GPU processing stages, exposing the constraints that govern completed inference throughput. Section 2: How Do You Map a Real-Time Edge AI Pipeline? Consider a laser-weeding system moving through a field. Cameras and LIDAR scan the plants ahead, AI determines which plants are weeds, and the machine directs a laser to the right location—all while the vehicle continues moving. The decision must arrive within a predictable time window. A delayed result is not merely slower computing; it can mean treating the wrong spot or missing the weed entirely. To model that workflow, begin with a network diagram: a map of the stages the data must pass through and the connections between them. Each stage performs useful work, has finite capacity, and can create a queue when demand arrives faster than it can be served. In factory terms, the sensor data is the incoming material, the connections are conveyors, memory is work-in-process storage, processors are work centers, and the weed classification and targeting command are the finished output. 1. Capture — the receiving dock. Cameras, LIDAR, and other sensors observe the crop row. An FPGA can collect and organize these high-speed inputs close to the sensors so the rest of the system receives data in a predictable form. 2. Homogenize — inspection and preparation. Software or dedicated hardware aligns timestamps, converts formats, filters noise, and combines sensor feeds. This turns several different input streams into a consistent set of frames or objects that the AI can use. 3. Transport — the conveyor system. The prepared data must reach GPU memory or high-speed storage. A direct PCIe path can avoid unnecessary trips through CPU memory, reducing processor overhead and traffic across shared processor interconnects such as QPI or UPI. 4A. Local inference — an on-site work center. The prepared data stays on the machine and moves across PCIe into a local GPU or inference accelerator. The result then travels directly to the laser-control system. 4B. Cloud inference — an external work center. Alternatively, selected data can be packaged for transmission through a NIC and 5G modem, sent across the mobile network to a cloud inference accelerator, processed remotely, and returned as a targeting decision. This branch adds an outbound transfer, network transit, cloud queue and processing time, and a return transfer before the machine can act. 5. Communicate, actuate, or store — shipping and records. A local result can be sent to the laser-control system, recorded to storage, or transmitted through a NIC to another system. For the cloud branch, the returned decision must move from the 5G modem through the control path before the laser can fire. These outbound and return paths consume bandwidth and add service time. 6. Software transport layers — the dispatch rules. Drivers, messaging frameworks, data-movement libraries, schedulers, network protocols, and cloud services coordinate the handoffs between stages. They determine what data is sent, what stays local, where work waits, and how much copying or retransmission occurs. Once the stages are visible, three practical constraints usually stand out: Sensor-ingest capacity: Multiple cameras and LIDAR feeds can produce data faster than the FPGA, Ethernet link, or switched fabric can accept it. The first queue forms before the AI sees a frame. CPU and system-memory staging: If each frame is first copied into CPU memory, prepared there, and then copied again to GPU memory, the CPU becomes an unnecessary handling station. The extra movement consumes memory bandwidth, processor time, and capacity on shared CPU interconnects such as QPI or UPI. PCIe path contention: Cameras, FPGA cards, GPUs, storage, and NICs may share PCIe lanes or a common switch uplink. Even when each device is fast on its own, the shared path can become the factory conveyor that limits the entire line. The design objective is to shorten and balance this path. Where the hardware and software stack support it, direct or peer-to-peer data movement can place prepared sensor data closer to GPU-accessible memory without unnecessary CPU staging. The benefit is not “zero copy” as a slogan; it is fewer handoffs, less traffic through constrained resources, and more predictable time from observation to laser command. The network diagram also makes measurement straightforward. At each stage, record the incoming data rate, effective service capacity, queue or buffer depth, and processing time. For local inference, follow the route through the FPGA, PCIe switches, GPU, storage, and laser controller. For cloud inference, also measure payload size, uplink and downlink capacity, network round-trip time, cloud queue time, remote processing time, and the variability of each interval. The path with the least remaining capacity—or the longest persistent queue—becomes the likely system constraint. Measure both paths against the same demand, capacity, handoffs, and end-to-end flow time. Throughput and delay then tell us how much work stays in flight, how much buffering it needs, and how often the system can meet the laser-control deadline. Figure 2. Local and cloud inference branches share sensor capture and preparation but introduce different transport, queueing, processing, and control-path constraints. Section 3: How Do Bandwidth and Latency Dictate Edge AI Memory? Bandwidth keeps up with arriving work. Latency determines whether that work finishes in time to matter. Think conveyor width versus transit time: we need enough of both to get from a sensor observation to a laser command before the machine passes the plant. Start with 48 cameras, each delivering an approximately 8 MB uncompressed image at 120 frames/s after FPGA processing and format conversion. For scale, a 3840 × 2160 image at one byte per pixel contains approximately 8.29 MB. Synchronize those 48 prepared frames and we have a 384 MB package arriving every 8.33 milliseconds. Send each complete package across the PCIe x16 path once, and the math is straightforward: 384 MB/package × 120 packages/s = 46.08 GB/s. That is before LIDAR or any other traffic joins the line. That workload devours bandwidth. A Gen5 x16 path with 52 GB/s of usable capacity runs at 88.6% utilization and takes approximately 7.38 milliseconds/package in serialization delay—the time spent transferring the package over the link. Move to Gen6 x16 at 104 GB/s and utilization drops to 44.3%, while serialization delay falls to approximately 3.69 milliseconds/package. We get a shorter transfer and more breathing room. Another option is to add an independent conveyor and dispatch work across both rather than move each lot faster. The multi-accelerator pool must handle 5,760 camera frames/s: 48 cameras at 120 frames/s, not 120 individual frames/s. Model the multi-GPU array as one aggregate work center that processes a complete package in 6 milliseconds, providing approximately 167 complete packages/s. At 120 packages/s, inference uses 72% of that capacity. Batch size, data placement, and tensor pre-processing determine how the work and latency are distributed across individual GPUs. Allow another 4 milliseconds for capture, preparation, queueing, and control, excluding PCIe transfer. Hold that allowance constant and add the 6 milliseconds of processing: sensor-to-command flow time comes to approximately 17.38 milliseconds with Gen5 or 13.69 milliseconds with Gen6. Successive packages overlap across stages, just as different lots move through different factory work centers at the same time. Little’s Law — stable-pipeline averagesAverage WIP = Average Throughput × Average Flow TimeWIP is measured in packages, throughput in packages per second, and flow time in seconds. For a hard real-time sensor design built around ping-pong double buffering—such as 360-degree situational awareness or robotics—the strict operational target is L < 2, or Work-In-Process < 2, with L representing average WIP. Two occupied buffers represent the familiar overlap: one frame transferring while the previous frame is processing. Under this two-buffer constraint, sustained L > 2 means the required work in flight exceeds the available slots. With continuous, fixed-rate video arrivals and no spare service capacity to drain the backlog, work queues and the system cannot catch up without dropping frames. Work-in-process, or WIP, is everything that has entered the pipeline but has not yet produced a command—including work being transferred or processed, not just work waiting in a queue. A fractional average does not mean a fractional package exists at one instant; it means the number in flight varies over time. Applying Little’s LawGen5: 120 packages/s × 0.01738 s ≈ 2.09 packagesGen6: 120 packages/s × 0.01369 s ≈ 1.64 packages Gen5 (L = 2.09) breaches the double-buffer threshold and forces queueing. Gen6 (L = 1.64) stays safely inside the L < 2 limit to preserve deterministic timing. That is the architectural advantage—not just a faster transfer, but less work tied up between observation and command. At 384 MB per package, this represents approximately 801 MB of input-equivalent WIP with Gen5 or 631 MB with Gen6. The faster conveyor reduces transfer time and material in flight. Physical buffers must also accommodate intermediate tensors, copies, and arrival bursts: average WIP is a starting point, not the final memory budget. Cloud Bandwidth — The External Shipping Lane The cloud path hits a much narrower shipping lane. Sending the full array requires 46.08 GB/s = 368.64 Gb/s before networking overhead—3,072 times the assumed 120 Mb/s usable uplink. Even reducing every camera frame to 100 kB leaves us with 5,760 frames/s × 100 kB = 576 MB/s = 4.608 Gb/s, still 38.4 times the uplink’s capacity. The machine has to select regions, features, or events locally before the external work center can keep up. Instead, let local processing select one 100 kB request from each complete 384 MB package. Now the uplink carries 120 requests/s × 100 kB = 12 MB/s = 96 Mb/s, using 80% of the assumed 120 Mb/s usable capacity. That fits, but it changes the division of work. The cloud handles a selected downstream task; the machine still does significant processing and data reduction. A task-specific request is not a compressed replacement for every original image. Remote compute cannot fix an undersized uplink. When incoming demand exceeds outgoing capacity, backlog grows even with negligible network transit time. A larger buffer only postpones overflow. We can increase connection capacity, send less data, reduce the incoming workload, or keep more processing local. The local PCIe constraint is a separate problem: Gen6 or a second independent Gen5 x16 link doubles that conveyor’s capacity and reduces balanced utilization from 88.6% to 44.3%. Both workflows start with a 384 MB sensor package at 120 packages/s. Producing the 100 kB cloud request takes a 3,840-to-one reduction, and the full 46.08 GB/s still has to reach the local reduction stage. Reads, writes, and intermediate copies can add more memory and interconnect traffic. Placement matters: FPGA-side selection can reduce downstream PCIe demand; GPU-side selection requires the full input to reach the GPU first. The bandwidth saving also carries an information tradeoff. A selected 100 kB request cannot preserve the complete 384 MB image package in this example: cropping can remove scene context, downsampling can reduce spatial resolution, and feature extraction can omit details that a different or future model might need. Lossless compression preserves information, but cannot be assumed to deliver this reduction. The cloud therefore works from a narrower representation, not the same full-resolution input available locally. The design decision is how much local bandwidth and processing to spend on reduction, what sensor detail to retain, and whether the resulting task performance justifies the uplink saving. In factory terms, shipping only selected material relieves the outbound lane, but inspection and sorting still need local capacity—and discarded material is unavailable to the external work center. Section 4: How Do You Manage Bottlenecks When AI Demand Varies? Average capacity is only the first test. Crop density and scene complexity can change inference work or the amount of selected data sent downstream, even when the prepared camera frames remain fixed at 8 MB. Retransmissions, scheduling, and competing devices can change the service available on a PCIe or network path. These variations create uneven demand and service times—and queues that an average bandwidth figure alone cannot describe. With a package arriving every 8.33 milliseconds and a fixed transfer time, Gen5 clears each package before the next one arrives. Barely. Its 7.38-millisecond transfer at 88.6% utilization leaves approximately 0.95 milliseconds of breathing room. Gen6 finishes in 3.69 milliseconds, leaving approximately 4.64 milliseconds. Bursts, competing transfers, and variable service times eat into that margin and force work to wait. Inference is already at 72% and the locally reduced cloud uplink at 80%, so relieving transport can move the traffic jam elsewhere. Add a second independent Gen5 x16 path and a shared queue can send the next complete package to whichever link is free, provided both reach the required destination. Each link supplies approximately 135.4 packages/s; together they provide approximately 270.8 packages/s, with 44.3% balanced utilization at 120 arriving packages/s. Each link is a service resource, not a separate computer. For variable traffic, model that pooled queue as M/M/2: two servers with Poisson arrivals and exponential service times. The synchronized camera stream supplies the regular-arrival baseline; the M/M/2 model addresses random arrivals and variable service. Two Gen5 links, whole-package dispatch: Each package still takes 7.38 milliseconds to transfer, but two packages can move concurrently, reducing contention. One Gen6 link: Each package transfers in 3.69 milliseconds. Two Gen5 links, striped package: Splitting one package evenly across both can also achieve approximately 3.69 milliseconds, but requires concurrent striping and reassembly—not the same whole-package M/M/2 model. Fixed camera assignment: Permanently assigning 24 cameras to each link creates two separate queues rather than one pooled queue. Equal aggregate bandwidth does not mean equal response time. Dispatch policy determines how much of that capacity the workload can actually use. The added conveyor must remain independent through the constrained stage. Two x16 device connections that converge on the same saturated switch uplink do not double end-to-end capacity. Think of an Ethernet switch: feed two sustained wire-speed inputs into a single output of identical bandwidth and twice as much traffic arrives as can leave. The backlog grows past any two-buffer limit, driving L > 2 in the lossless backlog model and triggering backpressure or dropped packets when finite buffers fill. The exact same oversubscription principle applies to PCIe switching, although PCIe uses flow control rather than Ethernet-style congestion drops. Switch bandwidth, endpoint connectivity, memory bandwidth, and downstream accelerator capacity must support the parallel paths. An edge AI platform must therefore be architected as a non-blocking fabric, where aggregate ingress bandwidth never oversubscribes the downstream egress paths to the GPU or host memory. Once transport is relieved, the constraint may move to inference or another work center. The practical design loop is to identify the constraint, add capacity or change dispatch at that stage, and then measure the complete flow again. Safety capacity: the equivalent of safety stock. A factory does not plan inventory only for average demand; it chooses a service level and carries protection against demand above that average. An Edge AI pipeline faces a similar decision. For independent, randomly arriving requests at a steady average rate, a Poisson distribution describes how many may arrive within a given interval. That can model event-triggered jobs or competing requests, rather than the regularly synchronized camera packages in our example. Spare link and accelerator capacity provide the safety margin, while buffers absorb short bursts. Unlike inventory on a shelf, however, a real-time decision expires: extra buffering cannot rescue a result delivered after its deadline. The equivalent of a stockout is a missing, dropped, or late decision. The target is therefore an on-time service level, not simply machine uptime—for example, delivering 99.9% of required decisions before their deadlines over a defined operating period. A demand percentile alone does not establish that result: existing backlog, service times, parallel paths, and the deadline also determine the outcome. Adding a second independent PCIe path becomes a service-level investment, not merely a bandwidth upgrade. The queueing model connects variable demand and available service capacity to the probability of delivering useful work on time. The relevant design target is therefore not simply average bandwidth or average inference time. It is the probability that the complete sensor-to-command path meets its deadline. For a laser-weeding machine, the team should measure median and tail latency, queue depth by stage, dropped or stale frames, retransmissions, and the percentage of targeting decisions delivered before the plant leaves the laser’s effective window. This also changes how optimization work is prioritized. If the PCIe switch uplink limits sustained throughput, increasing GPU throughput alone will not raise the line’s output. For a transport constraint, compare faster links with additional independent x16 paths and the scheduling needed to use them. For a cloud-uplink constraint, compare greater connection capacity with local selection or compression that reduces outgoing demand. Operations management evaluates each improvement against the current throughput constraint, then checks whether the constraint has moved. Meeting the response deadline requires a separate analysis of cumulative latency. Figure 3. One Gen5 x16 path, two pooled independent Gen5 x16 paths, and one Gen6 x16 path offer different transfer times and dispatch options, with inference at 72% utilization becoming a potential next constraint. Section 5: What Does Bottleneck Analysis Change About Edge AI Design? Modeling an Edge AI pipeline as a factory floor changes the question from “Which component is fastest?” to “Which stage limits the complete flow?” A network diagram reveals the handoffs. Capacity analysis exposes the constrained lanes and links. Little’s Law translates delay into work-in-process and buffer demand. Queuing theory explains both the cost of high utilization and the value of parallel service resources. A faster conveyor and a second conveyor are different design choices; topology and dispatch determine which one best protects the flow. For the laser-weeding example, the bandwidth comparison makes the feasible division of work visible. The complete camera array requires 368.64 Gb/s, far beyond the assumed 120 Mb/s cloud uplink. Selecting one 100 kB request per complete package reduces demand to 96 Mb/s, but changes the cloud’s role to processing selected information rather than the full array. This is the shipping-lane constraint: remote processing capacity cannot compensate for a connection that cannot sustain the incoming data rate. The payoff is a different investment decision. With one Gen5 link, transport uses 88.6% of capacity and inference uses 72%. Add an independent Gen5 link or upgrade to Gen6, and transport falls to 44.3%; inference is now the more heavily loaded of those two work centers. The next improvement belongs at the new constraint, not automatically at the newest or fastest component. Bandwidth and latency are different tests. Little’s Law translates flow time into work-in-process; comparing local and cloud response times requires the elapsed time along each complete path. Capture, preparation, transfer, processing, and control add time wherever one step waits for another. Overlapping successive packages can keep throughput high without shortening any individual package’s trip. A factory can hit its production rate and still miss a delivery promise. So can this pipeline. Add up processing, handoffs, waiting, and network delays—and check the slowest responses, not just the average. Both hardware and software determine that result. Hardware supplies the lanes, memory bandwidth, parallel work centers, and connectivity; software determines how work reaches them through scheduling, batching, queue management, data placement, and synchronization. More links cannot help if software funnels every transfer through one path, and better scheduling cannot create bandwidth that the hardware does not provide. Protecting the flow means designing the physical factory and its dispatch rules together. For OSS, that translates into concrete design questions: Do rugged PCIe interconnects and switch fabrics provide independent paths where the workload needs them? Can GPUs, NVMe storage, and high-speed NICs exchange data without avoidable staging? Can the thermal architecture sustain that capacity under real operating conditions? These are not separate specification checks; together, they determine whether the pipeline keeps work moving. The math behind operations management has not changed. The factory floor is now a stream of sensor data moving through lanes, memory, accelerators, networks, and control systems—and the best architecture is the one that protects the flow.

**46.08 GB/s** still has to reach the local reduction stage. Reads, writes, and intermediate copies can add more memory and interconnect traffic. Placement matters: FPGA-side selection can reduce downstream PCIe demand; GPU-side selection requires the full input to reach the GPU first.


****


The bandwidth saving also carries an information tradeoff. A selected 100 kB request cannot preserve the complete 384 MB image package in this example: cropping can remove scene context, downsampling can reduce spatial resolution, and feature extraction can omit details that a different or future model might need. Lossless compression preserves information, but cannot be assumed to deliver this reduction. The cloud therefore works from a narrower representation, not the same full-resolution input available locally. The design decision is how much local bandwidth and processing to spend on reduction, what sensor detail to retain, and whether the resulting task performance justifies the uplink saving. In factory terms, shipping only selected material relieves the outbound lane, but inspection and sorting still need local capacity—and discarded material is unavailable to the external work center.


# Section 4: How Do You Manage Bottlenecks When AI Demand Varies?


Average capacity is only the first test. Crop density and scene complexity can change inference work or the amount of selected data sent downstream, even when the prepared camera frames remain fixed at 8 MB. Retransmissions, scheduling, and competing devices can change the service available on a PCIe or network path. These variations create uneven demand and service times—and queues that an average bandwidth figure alone cannot describe.


With a package arriving every 8.33 milliseconds and a fixed transfer time, Gen5 clears each package before the next one arrives. Barely. Its


**7.38-millisecond** transfer at


**88.6% utilization** leaves approximately


**0.95 milliseconds** of breathing room. Gen6 finishes in


**3.69 milliseconds** , leaving approximately


**4.64 milliseconds** . Bursts, competing transfers, and variable service times eat into that margin and force work to wait. Inference is already at ****


**72%** and the locally reduced cloud uplink at


**80%** , so relieving transport can move the traffic jam elsewhere.


Add a second independent Gen5 x16 path and a shared queue can send the next complete package to whichever link is free, provided both reach the required destination. Each link supplies approximately 135.4 packages/s; together they provide approximately 270.8 packages/s, with


**44.3% balanced utilization** at 120 arriving packages/s. Each link is a service resource, not a separate computer. For variable traffic, model that pooled queue as


M/M/2


: two servers with Poisson arrivals and exponential service times. The synchronized camera stream supplies the regular-arrival baseline; the M/M/2 model addresses random arrivals and variable service.


- **Two Gen5 links, whole-package dispatch:** Each package still takes


**7.38 milliseconds** to transfer, but two packages can move concurrently, reducing contention.


- **One Gen6 link:** Each package transfers in


**3.69 milliseconds** .


- **Two Gen5 links, striped package:** Splitting one package evenly across both can also achieve approximately


**3.69 milliseconds** , but requires concurrent striping and reassembly—not the same whole-package M/M/2 model.


- **Fixed camera assignment:** Permanently assigning 24 cameras to each link creates two separate queues rather than one pooled queue.


Equal aggregate bandwidth does not mean equal response time. Dispatch policy determines how much of that capacity the workload can actually use.


The added conveyor must remain independent through the constrained stage. Two x16 device connections that converge on the same saturated switch uplink do not double end-to-end capacity. Think of an Ethernet switch: feed two sustained wire-speed inputs into a single output of identical bandwidth and twice as much traffic arrives as can leave. The backlog grows past any two-buffer limit, driving L > 2 in the lossless backlog model and triggering backpressure or dropped packets when finite buffers fill. The exact same oversubscription principle applies to PCIe switching, although PCIe uses flow control rather than Ethernet-style congestion drops. Switch bandwidth, endpoint connectivity, memory bandwidth, and downstream accelerator capacity must support the parallel paths. An edge AI platform must therefore be architected as a


**non-blocking fabric** , where aggregate ingress bandwidth never oversubscribes the downstream egress paths to the GPU or host memory. Once transport is relieved, the constraint may move to inference or another work center. The practical design loop is to identify the constraint, add capacity or change dispatch at that stage, and then measure the complete flow again.


**Safety capacity: the equivalent of safety stock.** A factory does not plan inventory only for average demand; it chooses a service level and carries protection against demand above that average. An Edge AI pipeline faces a similar decision. For independent, randomly arriving requests at a steady average rate, a Poisson distribution describes how many may arrive within a given interval. That can model event-triggered jobs or competing requests, rather than the regularly synchronized camera packages in our example. Spare link and accelerator capacity provide the safety margin, while buffers absorb short bursts. Unlike inventory on a shelf, however, a real-time decision expires: extra buffering cannot rescue a result delivered after its deadline.


The equivalent of a stockout is a missing, dropped, or late decision. The target is therefore an on-time service level, not simply machine uptime—for example, delivering 99.9% of required decisions before their deadlines over a defined operating period. A demand percentile alone does not establish that result: existing backlog, service times, parallel paths, and the deadline also determine the outcome. Adding a second independent PCIe path becomes a service-level investment, not merely a bandwidth upgrade. The queueing model connects variable demand and available service capacity to the probability of delivering useful work on time.


The relevant design target is therefore not simply average bandwidth or average inference time. It is the probability that the complete sensor-to-command path meets its deadline. For a laser-weeding machine, the team should measure median and tail latency, queue depth by stage, dropped or stale frames, retransmissions, and the percentage of targeting decisions delivered before the plant leaves the laser’s effective window.


This also changes how optimization work is prioritized. If the PCIe switch uplink limits sustained throughput, increasing GPU throughput alone will not raise the line’s output. For a transport constraint, compare faster links with additional independent x16 paths and the scheduling needed to use them. For a cloud-uplink constraint, compare greater connection capacity with local selection or compression that reduces outgoing demand. Operations management evaluates each improvement against the current throughput constraint, then checks whether the constraint has moved. Meeting the response deadline requires a separate analysis of cumulative latency.

# Section 5: What Does Bottleneck Analysis Change About Edge AI Design?


Modeling an Edge AI pipeline as a factory floor changes the question from “Which component is fastest?” to “Which stage limits the complete flow?” A network diagram reveals the handoffs. Capacity analysis exposes the constrained lanes and links. Little’s Law translates delay into work-in-process and buffer demand. Queuing theory explains both the cost of high utilization and the value of parallel service resources. A faster conveyor and a second conveyor are different design choices; topology and dispatch determine which one best protects the flow.


For the laser-weeding example, the bandwidth comparison makes the feasible division of work visible. The complete camera array requires 368.64 Gb/s, far beyond the assumed 120 Mb/s cloud uplink. Selecting one 100 kB request per complete package reduces demand to 96 Mb/s, but changes the cloud’s role to processing selected information rather than the full array. This is the shipping-lane constraint: remote processing capacity cannot compensate for a connection that cannot sustain the incoming data rate.


The payoff is a different investment decision. With one Gen5 link, transport uses 88.6% of capacity and inference uses 72%. Add an independent Gen5 link or upgrade to Gen6, and transport falls to 44.3%; inference is now the more heavily loaded of those two work centers. The next improvement belongs at the new constraint, not automatically at the newest or fastest component.


Bandwidth and latency are different tests. Little’s Law translates flow time into work-in-process; comparing local and cloud response times requires the elapsed time along each complete path. Capture, preparation, transfer, processing, and control add time wherever one step waits for another. Overlapping successive packages can keep throughput high without shortening any individual package’s trip. A factory can hit its production rate and still miss a delivery promise. So can this pipeline. Add up processing, handoffs, waiting, and network delays—and check the slowest responses, not just the average.


Both hardware and software determine that result. Hardware supplies the lanes, memory bandwidth, parallel work centers, and connectivity; software determines how work reaches them through scheduling, batching, queue management, data placement, and synchronization. More links cannot help if software funnels every transfer through one path, and better scheduling cannot create bandwidth that the hardware does not provide. Protecting the flow means designing the physical factory and its dispatch rules together.


For OSS, that translates into concrete design questions: Do rugged PCIe interconnects and switch fabrics provide independent paths where the workload needs them? Can GPUs, NVMe storage, and high-speed NICs exchange data without avoidable staging? Can the thermal architecture sustain that capacity under real operating conditions? These are not separate specification checks; together, they determine whether the pipeline keeps work moving.


The math behind operations management has not changed. The factory floor is now a stream of sensor data moving through lanes, memory, accelerators, networks, and control systems—and the best architecture is the one that protects the flow.
